  What changed in V3-PROMPT.md (now 8,017 words, generic, no system names in the
  rules; payments and Uber stay as the reference standard):

  - Measured style bands replace word limits. My earlier limits (90-word
    paragraph, 700-word hard part, 20-word recap line) were wrong: the reference
    pages have 180 to 230-word story paragraphs, hard parts up to 1,094 words
    and recap lines of 17 to 52 words. What actually separates Astra's page from
    the references is clipped rule-sentences (average 13 words vs 22 to 25),
    half the "because" rate, half the numbers, and 20 hedge words vs 0 to 4. The

    in full", rule 15 "one story per paragraph, not a rule list".
  - Black-box rule for any component whose insides are not the design (a model,
    a card network, a routing engine, a bank): only the facts the design uses.
  - No links, citations, paper or vendor names; name a technique once in bold.
  - Numbers must decide something the interviewer asks; Little's law defined;
    "measure it" banned as an answer; hedges at most five.
  - Cast = request path only; operators and suppliers are boxes. Names table and

  - Scoring by a fresh read, not by applied findings; a clean self-report with
    no stop list is treated as a skipped read-through.
  - Section 9 now has five failure/fix pairs from different systems (payments,
    chat, maps, a lease mechanism, a fleet sizing).

  New gate: hld/_wb/v3_lint.py <slug>. Runs on the built HTML, prints PASS/FAIL

⏺ Fair point, the earlier one was a report in Times, not a paper. Redone
  properly from the two papers you showed, opened for you:

  - LLM Inference - Paper Two Columns.pdf — the Dynamo look: US letter, Times
    10pt in two columns with the SOSP gutter, centred title with a byline, the
    problem statement opening the left column like an abstract, numbered
    sections in bold Arial like ACM, plain figures with "Figure 1:" captions,
    code set off by rules instead of boxes, push questions and the recap as
    plain lists. 21 pages.
  - LLM Inference - Paper One Column.pdf — the Attention look: NeurIPS width
    text block, centred title, narrower abstract block, bold numbered sections,
    centred figure captions. 25 pages.

  What I kept from our reading rules on purpose, because a reader beats a
  template: no hyphenated line ends, no box or code split across a column, the
  whole-design and reference diagrams at full width or on landscape pages rather
  than squeezed into one column like Dynamo's. The earlier "(Times)" pair is
  deleted so the folder has only these plus Astra's Charter pair.

  Permanent option for every page: python3 v3_latex.py <slug> --two-col --paper
  and python3 v3_latex.py <slug> --paper.

  What changed, against your comments

  - OTP before authorise, stated once. Start now has "The order, once": six
    numbered steps with times (create 40 ms, OTP 20 to 60 s, authorise about 1
    s, capture the same second, settle that night, pay out day 2) and says
    plainly that nothing is charged until the proof comes back. The two-clocks
    picture is redrawn with the OTP as phase 1 above the boxes. The no-OTP form
    is one sentence there and nowhere else.
  - Repetition removed. Cast is roles only. The design list describes what each
    arrow carries and nothing more. The sequence section is the picture plus two
    pushes; the vault paragraph moved into the data section, the no-OTP
    paragraph into Start.
  - Derivation rewritten as a derivation. Each of the nine questions now runs
    requirement, simplest thing, why it fails, the box it forces. Kafka is
    derived: call the merchant inline fails, publish inline fails, so outbox
    plus relay; and why a log and not a queue (three consumers, each needs every
    event, replayable). The inbox is derived as the outbox in reverse. The job
    scheduler appears as a box.
  - API fold uses real JSON request and response per call, trimmed to the fields
    that matter.
  - Data section rebuilt. A placement rule, a new picture of the five stores and
    the four flows between them, one bullet per store saying what, why, how it
    gets there, how long, and who reads it: Postgres tables including the
    per-day staging table; the vault with an HSM key and network tokens; Redis
    holding only losable things; ClickHouse events plus payments_daily written
    by the reporting consumer in batches; object storage with the monthly
    Parquet archive, its index and the account checkpoint. "How it is split" now
    lives here: the directory table in a control database with a version and 10
    s refresh, the routing library, hot-merchant detection (over 30% of a
    shard's writes, checked hourly) and the migration steps with logical
    replication, sub-shards for a giant.
  - Hard parts: architecture, fewer words each. Idempotency is one rule, one
    table, three steps, SQL, the race picture. UNKNOWN is the two cases and what
    each wrong choice costs. The sweeper is defined once as an Airflow task per
    shard every 30 s with a lock row. The ledger problem is what we are doing
    and why a column cannot; paisa explained as integers plus minor units.
    Events now name the topic, 64 partitions, key, retention, the three consumer
    groups with offsets, and how each recognises a repeat (unique delivery row,
    ReplacingMergeTree, idempotent mark), with a new picture. Reconciliation is
    split into two parts: "Proving the books" (the Postgres inbox with SKIP
    LOCKED and why not SQS; a night pipeline picture: SFTP, object storage,
    split by shard prefix, COPY into staging, match 1 as one join per shard,
    match 2 with batches defined, four kinds of break) and "Paying the merchant"
    (the payout SQL over the ledger, NEFT/RTGS/IMPS through the bank's API and
    why the card network is not involved, our reference, returns, chargebacks
    end to end, the reserve).
  - Part 3 keeps the failure table and what to watch. Six hard parts, eleven
    pictures, gate all pass.

  Roughly a quarter less to read, and the words that stayed are the specifics
  you asked for, not the narration.

  How the repetition went away
  - The flow of one payment is told exactly once, in "The order, once" (six
    numbered steps with times). The cast is roles only. The design list is
    fifteen arrow labels, one line each, no story. The sequence section is the
    picture plus two pushes. The derivation asks why each box exists and does
    not retell the flow. Nothing from the cast to the sequence diagram is said
    twice.

  How the hard parts got shorter without losing the architecture
  - Each part is now: the problem in two or three sentences, the picture, the
    mechanism with the specifics by name, the SQL, one limit, two pushes. The
    picture carries the flow; the prose carries only reasons.
  - Sizes: idempotency 390, states 530, ledger 540 (150 of it the entries
    table), events 480, reconciliation 620, payouts and chargebacks 450. They
    were 770 to 1,000 before.
  - The folds shrank too: derivation nine questions at about 45 words each, the
    API table as JSON, nine choices, four extra questions instead of six.

  Brief updated so this cannot happen again: the count that matters is the
  build's "with folds" number, at most 7,500, with at most 6,000 on the path and
  about 600 per hard part; adding a specific means cutting a sentence
  elsewhere.

  you read it; that number decides the budget for the other pages.

⏺ Payment gateway v3, third revision: built from the version you read, full

⏺ Sent. This one starts from the version you read and keeps its voice; I did not
  shorten sentences anywhere. What changed is structure and content.

  Repetition, fixed by structure, not by clipping
  - The flow is told once, in "The order, once" in Start: six numbered steps
    with times, and it says plainly that the OTP comes before the authorise and
    that nothing is charged until the proof comes back. The cast, the design
    list, the derivation and the sequence section refer to it instead of
    retelling it.
  - The derivation is real reasoning now: for each of nine requirements, the
    simplest design, why it fails, and the box that forces, in full sentences,
    including why Kafka and not a queue, and why an inbox table for the
    acquirer's webhooks.

  Design and architecture, given the same weight as functionality
  - New Part 3, about 1,800 words with a new picture: "Where it runs" (one
    region, three availability zones; each shard as primary plus synchronous
    standby in another zone plus a read replica; fencing and failover in about
    30 seconds; the vault, Kafka and caches placed the same way) and
    "Consistency, and what happens when a zone is cut off" (a table per store of
    what a reader gets and what a cut zone costs; the CAP choice stated
    plainly: the money path stops for the failover rather than accept two
    primaries, everything else stays available; and why every race on the page
    is settled by a durable row and a guard, never a lease in memory). Then
    failures, "How it grows" (pooling, splitting a shard through the directory,
    why the partition count is fixed) and what to watch.
  - The data section has the placement rule, the five-stores picture, one bullet
    per store, and the sharding mechanics (directory table, routing library,
    hot-merchant move by logical replication).
  - The hard parts keep the original prose and add the specifics you asked for:
    topic, 64 partitions, three consumer groups and how each recognises a
    repeat, the scheduler, the inbox with SKIP LOCKED and why not SQS, SFTP,
    batches defined, the bank rails for payouts, chargebacks end to end. Payouts
    are their own section.

  Length, counting folds: 10,400 on the path, 12,900 with folds, against the
  10,100 you read. The extra is Part 3; the repetition that was cut paid for the
  specifics. The brief now says length is controlled by telling each fact once
  and by pictures, never by shortening sentences, and Part 3 architecture is
  mandatory for every page.

⏺ Sent. Both asks done.

  The derivation, rethought. It is no longer "requirement, box". It is the nine
  questions a strong engineer actually asks, in the order they ask them, and the
  boxes fall out:
  1. What must never be wrong, and what may be stale.
  2. Who is outside my control, and what do they do to me (the merchant retries,
     the buyer takes a minute or abandons, the acquirer is slow, silent, keeps
     its own books, moves money at night and pulls it back; the regulator
     forbids card numbers). Most boxes turn out to be reactions to these five
     facts.
  3. What is the one record, and where does it live.
  4. Draw the happy path, with its clock.
  5. Walk every arrow: lost, silent, repeated, dies half way.
  6. After the commit, who needs to know, and how do I tell them without lying.
  7. What does the outside world tell me later, and how do I take it in safely.
  8. How does money leave, exactly once.
  9. Only now, the numbers.

  Three columns: the question, the answer for a payment gateway, what it puts in
  the picture. The three-stage picture's titles follow the questions. The first
  two rows come from the problem statement alone, which is the point for an
  interview or a blank page at work.

  Read 1 file, ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Payment gateway v3: derivation rewritten as one rule, then the simplest design
  broken one fact at a time (Fact, Break, Add), twelve moves, numbers last.

  › [file] ~/answers/hld/payment-v3.html (221.8KB)

⏺ Sent. The derivation is now something you can run yourself at a whiteboard.

  The shape
  - One rule before any box: decide what must never be wrong (was the buyer
    charged; what do we owe each merchant) and what may lag (a dashboard, a
    webhook). Never-wrong things go in one store a single transaction can
    protect; everything else is derived and allowed to be late.
  - Start from the simplest thing that could work: one service, one table, call
    the acquirer, answer yes or no.
  - Break it with one fact at a time. Twelve numbered moves, each with three
    labelled parts: Fact (from the problem statement, or how an outside party
    behaves), Break (the one way the board so far fails), Add (the one box, row,
    state or rule that fixes it, and why). For example: the OTP takes a minute,
    so the merchant's call cannot stay open, so answer pending and finish by
    webhook, and from here everything after the first commit is asynchronous.
    Or: a server dies mid-payment, so whatever it held is gone, so add nothing
    and make the row the memory.
  - Numbers last, and they multiply and split boxes rather than adding them.
  - The three-stage picture is captioned as "the board after moves 1 to 5, after
    6 to 9, after 10 and 11".

  Why this form: each step starts from something an average engineer can see in
  the statement, produces one visible thing on the board, and says its because
  aloud. The two earlier forms failed for the opposite reason, they presumed the
  answer.

  The brief now prescribes fact, break, add for every page, and records the two
  rejected forms so they do not come back. Page is 7,592 on the path, 9,611 with
  folds.

  Examples of the reasoning now in it:
  - Never charge twice: the memory of "have I seen this request" has three
    possible homes; in-process memory dies with the server; Redis SETNX can drop
    its last writes on failover, which is exactly a double charge, and is a
    second system that must agree with the database; a key row in the same
    transaction as the payment can never disagree and lets the unique index pick
    the winner. So the database, and the servers become stateless as a
    consequence.
  - Tell the merchant: why not call the merchant in the request, why not publish
    in the request (both holes), so the outbox and relay; then why Kafka and
    not SQS: three consumers each need every event, each at its own pace,
    replayable after a bug, in order per payment, and a queue hands each message
    to one consumer and deletes it.
  - The bank may not answer: why UNKNOWN is a state and not a retry, why a
    periodic job and not the request handler, why every bank call carries our
    own reference, why a second acquirer behind a circuit breaker.
  - The bank talks back: why an inbox table and not a queue product. Match the 
    bank's version: why the file and not webhooks, why two matches, why a breaks
    list for people rather than an auto-fix. Pay the merchant: why from the
    ledger and not from events, why our own reference, why a scheduler.

⏺ I've rebuilt the derivation around one method: start from the simplest design,

  This is how I would actually do it, in an interview or at work:

  1. Draw the simplest design that does the five jobs. A small picture shows it.
     One requirement changes it straight away: the OTP takes up to a minute, so
     the API answers "pending" and a webhook brings the result later.
  2. Test it against everything that could break it. The tests come from the
     promises in the requirements, such as "never charge twice" or "not one
     rupee lost". They also come from walking one payment and asking at each
     step whether it can be slow, silent, doubled, cut halfway or raced.
  3. When a test breaks the design, list the usual fixes for that kind of 
     problem, and let one detail of this system pick. This is the thinking the
     earlier versions lacked. For example, to stop a double charge you can
     remember the request key in memory, in Redis, or in the database. Memory
     dies with the server and a Redis failover can drop writes, so the key goes
     in the database, in the payment's own transaction.

  There are 14 tests, in the order a payment meets them, with scale and data
  centres last. The table's three columns are: the test and what breaks, the
  usual fixes, and what decides it here. A final board shows the finished design
  with each box tagged by the tests that shaped it. Seven of the tags land on
  the payments database.

  what happens instead of reading paragraphs. I've sent the page; it's also in

  Each step block has four parts:
  - Header: the step on the left, and on the right in green, "adds" plus the
    parts it adds to the design, so you can see the design grow step by step.
  - What it builds: one flow line, with the new parts in green. For example:
    merchant ──POST──▶ API gateway ──▶ payment service ──▶ payments DB.
  - Each thing that can go wrong, as two flows:
    - ✗ the obvious way, with where it breaks in red. For example: merchant
      ──charge──▶ us, charged ──reply──✗ lost, merchant resends ──▶ us: charged
      again.
    - ✓ what we do instead, with what it adds in green. For example: merchant
      ──charge, key K1──▶ us ──INSERT K1──▶ keys table, and on the resend,
      "INSERT K1 refused ──▶ the stored reply: no second charge".
  - Why: one grey sentence, only where the reason isn't already visible in the
    flows.

  Some steps draw small pictures, such as two servers racing into "both capture"
  in step 4, and Kafka branching to its three readers in step 5.

  The first principles. The fold's intro names five facts no design can change,
  and every step's chain is built from them:
  - A call can fail after the other side already acted.
  - A machine can die between any two writes.
  - Memory is lost on restart.
  - Two machines can act on the same thing at the same moment.
  - The bank keeps its own books.

  What a chain looks like. Step 2 reads:
  1. The merchant can't tell a lost reply from a lost request, so it will retry,
     and we will receive some charges twice.
  2. So a retry must be recognisable as the same charge. Only something the
     merchant sends both times can do that: an idempotency key, chosen once per
     order.
  3. The key must be remembered as long as the charge exists, even when the
     server that saw it dies. Memory dies with that server, and a Redis failover
     can drop writes.
  4. The charge's own row already survives all of that. So the key goes into the
     payments database, under a unique index.

  The link to the picture. The component each chain arrives at is written in
  green, the same green as its new box in the picture.

  The "How it works" and "Why it is built this way" blocks are gone. The events
  section no longer repeats the outbox reasoning; it points to step 5 instead.
  The page passes the checks, and the brief now requires this chain form for
  every future system.

❯ not just that diagrams also shit, any other way to think in terms of mental   
  models or something, in general when designing my systems in our office or    
  work, I see my seniors thinking like this mental models                       

⏺ Yes. Seniors don't derive a design from scratch each time. They carry a small
  set of mental models, notice which ones a problem triggers, and let each one
  force part of the design. For payments, eight of them produce the whole
  picture:

  1. One source of truth; everything else is a copy. Keep whatever must never be
     wrong in one store and one transaction. Everything else is fed from it and
     may lag. Here, Postgres holds the payment, its key and its ledger entries
     together. Webhooks, dashboards and payouts read copies through the outbox
     and Kafka.
  2. Every call can arrive twice, so every receiver must shrug off a repeat.
     Replies get lost and callers retry. Here, that gives the merchant's
     idempotency key, our reference on bank calls and payouts, and event ids for
     the Kafka readers. It also gives the inbox for the bank's callbacks.
  3. A timeout is not a failure. After a timeout you don't know what happened,
     so you never guess: you record "unknown" and go and ask. Here, that is the
     UNKNOWN state and the sweeper.
  4. The core object is a state machine. Every change is a move between named
     states, allowed only from the right state. Here, that is the payment's
     states and the guarded UPDATE.
  5. Make wrongness visible. Keep a rule that must always hold, so a bug shows
     up as a broken rule. Here, that is double entry: the two sides must always
     total the same.
  6. If someone else keeps books, check against theirs. Here, that is the
     nightly reconciliation against the bank's settlement file, with mismatches
     going to a breaks list for people.
  7. Keep dangerous things in a small box, and slow things off the fast path.
     Here, the card vault and tokens keep card numbers in a small box. Answering
     "pending" at once keeps the minute-long OTP off the fast path, and the
     router keeps a sick bank off it too.
  8. Split along the line your transactions never cross, and copy what you can't
     lose. Here, that is sharding by merchant, plus a synchronous standby for
     every shard.

  These eight carry over to other systems. A ride-hailing or ticket-booking
  design triggers most of the same models; only the components change. That's
  the part worth learning.

  On the page, the derivation could become these models instead of nine timeline
  frames. Each model would get its one-line rule and the parts of the design it
  forces, marked on the single design picture you like. I've stopped the edit I
  was making and haven't changed the page for this yet. I can draft one model
  in that form for you to check before redoing the rest.

  Read 1 file (ctrl+o to expand)

  models above produce the whole payment design, and most of them carry over to

  The overview. One table lists all eight models, each with what it forces in
  this design.

  Each model has the same five parts. Models 1 and 2 are worked in full:
  - The rule, in yellow. For example: "Anything sent over a network may arrive
    twice, so every receiver needs a key that recognises a repeat."
  - Why it is true. One or two sentences from first principles. For model 2: a
    lost reply looks like a lost request, so the sender must resend, and no two
    machines can promise exactly once.
  - Your design picture, with only this model lit up. The rest is dimmed.
    - Model 1 shows the truth in green: the payments database, the one
      transaction and the card vault. The copies fed from it are in blue.
    - Model 2 lights the six places a message can arrive twice, numbered 1 to 6:
      the merchant's charge, our bank calls, Kafka events, the bank's
      callbacks, payouts and our webhooks.
  - A table of exactly where it lands. For model 2, each numbered hop gets its
    key: the idempotency key, our reference T1, the event id, the inbox, payout
    reference N123, and the merchant storing our event id.
  - Spot it in any system. One line you can reuse elsewhere. For model 2: for
    every arrow, ask what happens if it arrives twice, and name the key that
    makes the second one harmless.

⏺ I've rewritten the derivation in your office LLM's style. It's the fold under
  the design picture: "How to arrive at this design: one payment, nine 
  questions" (open in your browser and sent to you).

  What it looks like:
  - One dark terminal panel, all in monospace. Section headings are purple and
    the numbered items are orange.
  - Short plain sentences, written as if someone is talking to you.
  - Small top-to-bottom box diagrams, with the reason written beside each box
    after ◀──.
  - What goes wrong is shown as short arrow chains, like reply lost ──▶ merchant
    resends ──▶ looks new ──▶ charged twice ✗.
  - The tempting options sit in lined-up rows, each ending in ✗ or ✓. Each item
    ends with one takeaway line.
  - Colour is used only for meaning: the boxes a step adds are green, so you can
    see what each step changes in the design.

  What's inside:
  1. A short opening that gives the method: walk one payment through the system,
     and at every hop ask "what can go wrong here?"
  2. A map of the 9 hops, with that question written next to each.
  3. One numbered item per hop.
  4. A closing "And the rest?", which points out that steps 2, 5, 6 and 8 are
     the same trick: give each message a name, so a repeat does nothing.

  There's no before/after structure. The old "mental models" draft is gone, and
  the rest of the page is unchanged.

  If this reads well, I'll convert the six hard-part sections into the same
  style next.

⏺ I've rebuilt the derivation so it builds the design instead of touring it.
  Same terminal format; open the fold "How to arrive at this design: five jobs, 
  one checklist".

  How it works:
  - A checklist of six "what if?" questions, taken from the requirements: a
    server dies halfway, the bank is slow or silent, the same request arrives
    twice, a rupee goes missing, it touches a card number, it must hold 3,000 a
    second.
  - The interviewer's jobs, one at a time: take a payment, never charge twice,
    refund, tell the merchant, pay the merchant with books that match the
    bank's, then the numbers.
  - Each job goes the same way:
    a. The simplest thing that does it, shown as a tiny naive flow. For "never
       charge twice" that is: look up the order, and if it's found, send the old
       answer.
    b. The checklist run on it: what breaks (✗), then what changes (✓).
    c. The whole design redrawn, with what this job added in green. Boxes keep
       their places, so you watch the picture grow from 4 boxes to the full
       design.

  Later steps build on earlier decisions:
  - The sweeper from step 1 also clears stuck idempotency keys in step 2.
  - The ledger in step 5 joins "the same transaction" that already holds the
    outbox row.
  - Step 6 splits the database by merchant because splitting by payment id would
    break step 5's transaction.

  It's in ~/Downloads/payment-v3.html and I've sent it to you.

  The method (it works for any system): take the requirements in the order they
  bite. For each one:
  - write the obvious way to meet it,
  - ask why it fails against what the system must survive,
  - add what fixes it.

  For payments that's 10 rows, e.g. "Never charge twice" → remember requests in
  server memory or Redis → a retry lands on another server, and a Redis failover
  drops writes → an idempotency key under a unique index in the payments DB.
  Later rows build on earlier ones, like "in the same transaction" or "every
  transaction stays on one machine". The sentences are full but short.

  What answers your real problem, "I can't remember 50 designs": a second small
  table, "Carry this to any system." The why it fails column keeps repeating the
  same few reasons, and each has one standard fix:

  ┌───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ the obvious way fails │                the standard fix                 │
  │        because        │                                                 │
  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ a crash lands between │ put both in one transaction                     │
  │  two writes           │                                                 │
  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ a retry looks like a  │ the caller names the request; a unique index    │
  │ new request           │ refuses the repeat                              │
  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ a timeout hides       │ an "unknown" state, and a job that asks until   │
  │ whether the call      │ it knows                                        │
  │ worked                │                                                 │
  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ something slow sits   │ answer now, finish later from a saved row       │
  │ on the request path   │                                                 │
  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ your records drift    │ compare with theirs on a schedule               │
  │ from someone else's   │                                                 │
  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ dangerous data        │                                                 │
  │ spreads to every      │ keep it in one small box, pass a token          │
  │ server                │                                                 │
  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ one machine can't     │ split by the key that keeps each transaction on │
  │ hold it, or can die   │  one machine, and copy each piece synchronously │
  └───────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  For a new system you don't recall anything. You list its requirements, write
  the obvious way for each, check it against these seven, and apply the matching
  fix. Read-heavy systems add a few more (caches, read replicas, search
  indexes), found the same way.

  › [file] ~/Downloads/payment-v3.html (207KB)

⏺ I've added the pros and cons, merged into the rows the way you liked. Every
  row where a real choice was made now ends with a short "X, not Y." line. It
  says what the other option does better, why it loses here, and what our pick
  costs us:

  - Kafka, not RabbitMQ or SQS.
    - SQS is the easiest to run, and RabbitMQ routes messages flexibly.
    - But a queue deletes a message once it's read, so three readers need three
      copies and nothing can be replayed after a bug.
    - Kafka keeps every event for days, each reader keeps its own place, and it
      keeps each payment's events in order.
    - It costs a cluster to run.
  - Postgres, not Cassandra or DynamoDB.
    - Those two grow across machines by themselves.
    - But Cassandra has no transactions across partitions, DynamoDB caps a
      transaction at 100 items and charges double, and neither can do the
      nightly check against the bank as one SQL join.
    - Postgres costs us sharding it ourselves, and MySQL would do just as well.
  - The other ten:
    - webhook and GET, rather than only one of them
    - idempotency keys in Postgres, not Redis
    - asking the bank, not waiting for it
    - a conditional update, not a lock
    - an outbox, not change data capture
    - ClickHouse, not a Postgres copy
    - an inbox table, not a queue
    - Airflow, not cron
    - splitting the database by merchant, not by payment id or consistent
      hashing
    - a synchronous standby, not an asynchronous one or a second active region

  The reusable table now has a "what it costs" column, because every pattern has
  a price. For example, sharding makes queries across keys hard, and a
  synchronous copy makes every commit wait.

  The fold is now about 1,700 words, and no new repeats with the rest of the
  page showed up. I've saved this as the derivation template for the other 50
  systems.

⏺ My honest take: the page is close but not perfect. The weak spots are the few
  paragraphs that tell a sequence of events in prose. I've made a pilot where
  only those become ASCII diagrams, so you can compare it side by side with the
  approved page.

  Why ASCII diagrams at work click and paragraphs don't: a paragraph describing
  a race or a crash-and-retry makes you hold the order of events in your head
  while you read. Someone else did the work of laying out that order. In an
  ASCII diagram, the arrows and the two side-by-side lanes (one per server) hold
  the order for you. Your eyes just follow it.

  My recommendation: use ASCII only where the prose tells a sequence or a race.
  I wouldn't redo everything.
  - The pictures stay. They show how the system is laid out, and you already
    approved them.
  - The tables stay, because they carry facts.
  - The problem stories stay, because they're short.

  On this page that's five paragraphs, and those are what the pilot converts:
  1. Section 06 (never charge twice), the gap where a server dies halfway: the
     server claims the key, then dies. The sweeper asks the bank, then either
     finishes the payment or releases the key so the merchant's retry can claim
     it.
  2. Section 07 (payment states), the capture race: a two-lane timeline for
     server A and server B. "Read in code, then write" ends in "captured twice
     ✗". A guarded UPDATE ends with the second server getting "0 rows ✓".
  3. Section 09 (telling the merchant), the two ways an event arrives twice: the
     relay dies before marking a row sent, or a worker dies before saving its
     place.
  4. Section 10 (proving the books), the bank's callbacks: the receiver saves
     each event into an inbox table, and several workers each take a different
     row.
  5. Section 12 (running it), a zone cut off from the network: without a lease
     you get two primaries ✗; with a lease you get 30 seconds of no writes ✓.

  The pilot is ~/Downloads/payment-v3-ascii.html; your approved payment-v3.html
  is untouched. Say which one reads better. If the pilot wins, I'll adopt it and
  use the same rule for the other HLDs.

❯ buddy How to derive this design yourself                                      
  this is amazing thank you so much for this, I guess this is how people will   
  think na when designing ?                                                     

⏺ Yes. This is genuinely how good engineers design: for each requirement, try
  the simplest thing, find what breaks, and apply the known fix. Interviewers
  are listening for exactly that loop, because it shows you understand why each
  box exists.

  In practice it differs from the table in three ways:

  - Seniors skip steps. They've hit "a retry charges twice" so often that they
    jump straight to the idempotency key. The "Carry this to any system" table
    is basically what's in their heads. You're building that same memory, just
    deliberately instead of through years of incidents.
  - Real design loops back. The table reads top to bottom, but a late
    requirement can change an early decision. In payments, the scale row (shard
    by merchant) exists because of an earlier row: the ledger has to commit in
    the same transaction as the payment. On a whiteboard you'll often go back
    and redraw.
  - The first idea is often the right answer, for a smaller system. A startup
    doing 1,000 payments a day doesn't need Kafka or eight shards; one Postgres
    plus polling is fine. The senior skill is knowing when a fix is worth its
    cost. That's what the "X, not Y" lines and the "what it costs" column are
    teaching.

  At work you'd also weigh things interviews don't ask about: what your team
  already runs, cost, and deadlines. That's why two good engineers can end up
  with different designs.

  To make it yours, practise it on a system you haven't studied. List the
  requirements, then fill in "first idea / what goes wrong / what we do instead"
  without looking. Want me to give you one tomorrow and grade your table?

⏺ The derivation is rebuilt: two tables, functional and non-functional, with 10
  rows instead of 14. It's the same fold, "How to derive this design yourself",
  and I've sent you the updated page.

  Functional: what it must do (rows follow the interviewer's jobs)
  - F1. Take a payment: reply pending, then a webhook or GET.
  - F2. Never charge twice: the idempotency key. The API gateway moves here too,
    since it stops a merchant stuck in a retry loop, so it's no longer an
    unexplained "every API has one" box.
  - F3. Capture and refund: the guarded update, plus the inbox for the bank's
    later news (refunds finishing, chargebacks).
  - F4. Tell the merchant, and everyone inside: the whole flow in one row. The
    outbox row commits with the change, the relay publishes it to Kafka, and
    three consumer groups each read every event: the webhook sender, reporting
    into ClickHouse, and the payout planner.
  - F5. Keep books that balance: now a proper row. A balance column can't tell
    ₹2,499 still owed by the acquirer from ₹2,499 already in our escrow account.
    Double entry fixes that with the worked example: +2,499 owed by the
    acquirer = +2,440 merchant + ₹50 fee + ₹9 GST, both sides always equal, all
    in the payment's own transaction. That's why the database is Postgres.
  - F6. Match the bank, and pay the merchant: reconciliation, the breaks list,
    the payout job with our own reference, and the scheduler.

  Non-functional: what it must survive (each row stress-tests the design so far)
  - N1. Card numbers off our servers: the vault and tokens.
  - N2. A bank that is slow, silent or down: the UNKNOWN state, the sweeper, and
    a second acquirer behind a router.
  - N3. Our own server dying halfway: this row is new. Servers keep nothing in
    memory; every step is saved as a row before the next call, so any server can
    take over a retry.
  - N4. 3,000 a second, 36 TB a year, 99.99%: shards by merchant, plus a
    synchronous standby in a second zone.

  All the "X, not Y" comparisons are kept. The reusable table now points to rows
  by F/N number and has two new patterns: "one client can flood you" and "a
  server can die mid-request". The page checker is clean, with 0 failures and 0
  warnings. The fold grew from about 1,700 to about 2,150 words, mostly from the
  fuller ledger and tell-everyone rows.

⏺ I've rebuilt Part 3 around the questions interviewers actually ask about
  running a payment system, and sent you the updated page. It's four sections
  now instead of one long one:

  12. Where it runs: one region, three zones. Starts with plain definitions:
  - a region is one city where the cloud has data centres (Mumbai);
  - a zone is one of those buildings, with its own power and network, about a
    millisecond from the others.

  Then the zones picture and a "what runs where" table. The pushes: why three
  zones and not two (the third one breaks the tie when two lose contact), and
  why not two regions (a synchronous copy there adds tens of milliseconds to
  every commit).

  13. Consistent or available: the CAP choice, part by part. This is your
  friend's point. It explains CAP in one paragraph, then a table where each part
  makes its own choice:
  - the payments database and vault choose consistency: 30 seconds of errors
    beats two versions of who paid whom;
  - Kafka also chooses consistency, but nothing is lost because the outbox rows
    wait;
  - dashboards and caches choose availability, because late news costs nothing.

  Then the lease diagram as the concrete example, and a note that even without a
  network split, consistency costs about a millisecond per commit. Interviewers
  call that second trade-off PACELC. The pushes: why not fix conflicts later
  like a shopping cart, and what the merchant sees during those 30 seconds.

  14. When something breaks: 99.99%, failover and recovery.
  - 99.99% means a budget of 52 minutes a year. RPO is how much data you may
    lose; RTO is how long until you're back.
  - A new timeline diagram shows a primary dying, the standby promoted, and
    writes resuming in about 30 seconds with nothing lost.
  - A failure table covers everything from one server up to the whole region,
    with what merchants see, the recovery, the RPO and the RTO.
  - "Replication is not a backup": a bad UPDATE copies to the standby instantly,
    so each shard can also restore to any second before the mistake.

  15. How it grows, and how it is run.
  - A growth table: for each part, what runs out first, how it grows, and what
    changes at ten times the load.
  - What happens on a sale day above the plan, and how deploys and schema
    changes run with zero downtime.
  - A "watch / because / page someone when" table.

  One honest note: this is the right Part 3 for payments. Other systems will
  stress different things; a news feed, for example, cares more about caches and
  a few extremely popular accounts. So these four sections are the template,
  and each system gets its own content.

  The page checker is clean (0 failures, 0 warnings), nothing needs sideways
  scrolling, and the page is about 7,900 words. Excited for you too: once the
  other systems are in this shape, you'll be walking in with the same toolkit
  for every design.

⏺ Short answer: a mind map is for recollecting, not for storing. The page holds
  the information. The map holds cues, short prompts that help you pull the
  information back out of your own head. It only works if two things are true:
  the cues match what you'll be asked, and you practise the pulling.

  Why the current one "looks good after reading the doc" but won't work after 10
  days: it shows you the answers. Reading answers feels like knowing, because
  they're familiar, but an interviewer never shows you the answers; you have to
  produce them. After 10 days the familiarity fades, and what survives is what
  you practised recalling.

  What the map should be, for your goal of deriving the system and defending it:
  - A map of questions, not facts. Each node is a problem or a question, and its
    answer stays hidden until you click:
    - "a retry looks new → ?"
    - "the bank goes silent → ?"
    - "crash between the commit and the webhook → ?"
    - "why Kafka, not SQS?"

    You look at the cue, work out the fix in your head, then click to check.
  - In the order you'd present it in an interview: requirements → the flow of
    one payment → each problem and its fix → the numbers → running it. Recalling
    it in order is the same skill as defending it in order.
  - Numbers as prompts ("peak payments per second?", "storage a year?"), so you
    compute them instead of reading them.
  - As big as it needs to be, since you said size doesn't matter. Each hard part
    gets its full chain of cues.

  How it actually sticks: open it with the answers hidden on day 1, 3, 7 and 10,
  for about 10 minutes each time. Say each answer out loud, then click to
  check, and reread in the doc only what you missed. Your own learning guide
  already names this as your gap: you build maps but never test yourself.

  Want me to rebuild the mind map this way: questions visible, answers hidden,
  click to reveal, with a "show all" button for revision?

⏺ End fold is now "The technical round: nine questions interviewers push on".

  › [file] ~/Downloads/payment-v3.html (229.3KB)

⏺ The end section now asks only technical questions: "The technical round: nine 
  questions interviewers push on". The functionality questions are gone, and
  none of the nine repeat the questions already inside each section.

  1. Why not a two-phase commit across Postgres and Kafka, or a saga? Kafka
     can't join a Postgres transaction, so the outbox gets the same guarantee
     from one local commit. The payment is already a saga with the bank:
     authorise, then capture, with a void as the undo.
  2. Which isolation level? Plain READ COMMITTED is enough. Postgres makes a
     waiting UPDATE re-check its WHERE, so the second capture changes nothing.
  3. Why does the idempotency key commit on its own, first? So a retry during
     the bank call gets a 409 instead of charging again. The price is a small
     gap, which the sweeper closes.
  4. Kafka is down for an hour? Payments carry on, because events wait as outbox
     rows. Merchants hear an hour late but miss nothing, and the alarm is the
     age of the oldest unpublished outbox row.
  5. How do one payment's events stay in order, all the way to the merchant?
     Outbox ids run in order per shard, and the Kafka key is the payment id. A
     late webhook retry is harmless because GET is the truth.
  6. Is exactly-once possible? Not across two systems. We send at least once,
     and each reader remembers what it has seen in the same place it applies the
     event.
  7. Can the merchant read its own write right after a capture? Yes: GET reads
     the primary, and a promoted standby already has every confirmed commit.
  8. The shard key is the merchant, so how do you query across merchants? Not in
     Postgres. Those queries go to ClickHouse, which receives every event.
  9. What's the latency budget? About 40 ms to answer "pending". The bank's
     second and the buyer's OTP happen outside the request, which is why the
     answer is "pending".

❯ Kafka cannot join a Postgres transaction: its transactions cover only Kafka   
  itself, and a two-phase commit across two systems is slow and stalls whenever 
  either side is down. The outbox gives the same guarantee with one local       
  commit, and the relay delivers it at least once. A saga, a chain of steps     
  each with an undo, is what the payment already is with the bank: authorise,   
  then capture, with a void as the undo; inside our own system every change is  
  one local transaction, so nothing else needs one.

  understanding english balancing technical depth improve the wordings

  Here's the one you flagged, before and after.

  Before: "Kafka cannot join a Postgres transaction: its transactions cover only
  Kafka itself…"

  After:

  ▎ The goal is that a change and its news are saved together, or not at all. A 
  ▎ two-phase commit would make both systems agree first and then both save, but
  ▎ Kafka cannot take part in one, and it would make every payment wait on both
  ▎ systems and stop whenever either is down. The outbox gets the same result 
  ▎ with one ordinary commit: the news is just another Postgres row, and the 
  ▎ relay sends it to Kafka afterwards. A saga, a chain of steps where each step
  ▎ has an undo, is only needed when one change spans several systems; our one 
  ▎ such flow is with the bank, where a void undoes an authorisation.

  The other eight got the same treatment. For example:
  - Isolation level: "The row now says CAPTURED, so the second capture changes
    nothing."
  - Event ordering: "the same partition, a slice of the topic that a reader
    reads in order".
  - Exactly-once: "when an acknowledgement is lost, the sender cannot tell
    whether its message arrived, so it has to send again".

  nightly backup and its write-ahead log. Together they can restore the shard to
  any second before the mistake. We rehearse a restore every month."

  27. (a) "Each shard has a synchronous standby in a second zone: a commit is
  confirmed only once the standby has it." [N4]
  (b) "Zone" is only defined in Part 3, and N4's own heading calls the same
  thing "a data centre".
  (c) "Each shard has a synchronous standby in a second zone, a separate data
  centre in the same city with its own power and network. A commit is confirmed
  only once the standby has it." N4 heading: "even if a zone goes dark".

  28. (a) "Every payment writes the fee income row. Is that a hot row? Yes, and
  it is read rarely, so it is split into sixteen sub-rows" [ledger, interviewer
  bullet]
  (b) "Hot row" is not explained, and "it is read rarely, so it is split" skips
  the step that links the two halves.
  (c) "Every payment writes the fee income row. Is that a hot row, one that so
  many transactions update that they queue for its lock? Yes. Because the row is
  rarely read, we split it into sixteen sub-rows (fee_income_0 to
  fee_income_15): each entry adds to a random one, and a read adds the sixteen
  together. The per-merchant accounts stay single rows, because one merchant
  writes them a few times a second at most."

  29. (a) "Every movement is written as entries on two kinds of account, where
  the money is (the acquirer owes us, our escrow account)" [F7]
  (b) One sentence carries both kinds of account, two bracketed lists, the
  balancing rule and a worked example, and the cell then adds three more ideas.
  (c) "A double-entry ledger. Every movement of money is written as entries on
  two kinds of account. One kind says where the money is: 'acquirer owes us' or
  'our escrow account'. The other says whose it is: the merchant's, our fee, or
  GST. The two kinds always add up to the same total. For example, capturing
  ₹2,499 writes +2,499 to 'acquirer owes us', and +2,440 for the merchant, +50
  fee and +9 GST on the other side. A mistake shows up as totals that stop
  matching. The entries commit in the same transaction as the payment's new
  state. That needs transactions across rows, which is why the database is
  Postgres."

  30. (a) "The reserve held back from risky merchants exists for exactly this;
  beyond it, we invoice the merchant." [ledger, interviewer bullet]
  (b) The reserve is used as if the reader already knows it, but it is only
  explained two sections later.
  (c) "This is exactly what the reserve is for: the part of each payout that we
  hold back from risky merchants for 120 days (explained under 'Paying the
  merchant'). If the debt is larger than the reserve, we invoice the merchant."

  31. (a) "The company-wide accounts exist once per shard and are summed."
  [sharding table]
  (b) The reader is left to work out which accounts these are and when they are
  summed.
  (c) "Accounts that belong to the whole company, such as our fee income and GST
  payable, have one copy on each shard; to read one, we add up its eight

  32. (a) "The night is six tasks of the job scheduler, one task per shard where

  (b) "one task per shard where a shard is involved" reads like a riddle, and

  (c) "The night is six tasks run by the job scheduler. A task that works on the
  payments database runs once for each shard. The whole run must finish before
  the next day's file arrives."

  33. (a) "SFTP is file transfer over SSH, the standard in banking; our

  (b) Three unrelated rules share one cell, and the surprising fact that T1 is

  (c) "The acquirer puts the file on its SFTP server (SFTP is file transfer over

  34. (a) "events, one row per event, and a materialised view payments_daily per

  (b) "Materialised view" is not explained.
  (c) "events, with one row per event; and payments_daily, a materialised view:

  35. (a) "signed with an HMAC (a hash keyed by the endpoint's secret) of the

  (b) The bracket splits "an HMAC … of the body". In the retry cell, "after 1, 5

  hours.
  (c) "the event JSON, POSTed to the merchant's URL. We sign the body and a
  timestamp with an HMAC, a hash computed with the endpoint's secret, so the
  merchant can check that the webhook came from us and is recent." Rule: "The
  merchant must answer 200 within 10 seconds. If it does not, we retry after 1
  minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes and 2 hours, and keep retrying for 24 hours in
  all. After that the delivery is parked, and the merchant can replay it from
  its dashboard."

  36. (a) "401 wrong key; 402 the bank declined, with its reason code and a
  message safe to show the buyer; 409 the same key" [API, errors bullet]
  (b) Five error codes sit in one semicolon chain. "Key" is the API key in one
  item and the idempotency key in the next, and "the bank" here is the issuer.
  (c) "Few, and each says what to do. A 401 means the API key is wrong. A 402
  means the issuer declined; it carries the issuer's reason code and a message
  that is safe to show the buyer. A 409 means the same idempotency key is still
  in progress, or the payment is not in a state that allows this move, such as a
  second capture; the merchant should read GET. A 422 means the same
  idempotency key came with a different body, or a refund is larger than the
  capture. A 429 means slow down."

  37. (a) "keep 99.99% availability (when we are down, every merchant's checkout

  (b) Four requirements, a bracketed aside and a trailing "which PCI DSS …

  (c) "It must answer every API call fast. It must be available 99.99% of the

  never lose or invent a single rupee. And it must keep card numbers off our

  38. (a) "but Kafka cannot take part in one, and it would make every payment

  (b) "it" could be Kafka or the two-phase commit, and two separate objections

  (c) "A two-phase commit would make both systems agree first and then both

  (c) "Every event already flows into ClickHouse, which is built for questions

  (b) One paragraph mixes the transfer systems, the card network, the reserve

  (c) "The transfer is bank to bank, from our escrow account to the merchant's
  account, over the RBI's transfer systems: NEFT below ₹2 lakh, RTGS above, and
  IMPS for merchants on an instant plan. The card network is not involved,
  because it only moves money between the buyer's bank and the acquirer.

  These checks found no problems:
  - **Arithmetic:** 600/s, 1,800, 36 TB, 12,000 commits and 1,500 per shard,
  15,000 and 150,000 events, 250M outbox rows, 10M an hour, 52 minutes, fewer
  than 11 failovers, ₹2,499 = 2,440 + 50 + 9, 244000 paisa, 25M-row files.
  - **Timestamps:** 19:04:02, 19:04:47, 19:04:48, 19:04:50, 19:05:20.
